summary: Hidden Water Pulse maps the temporary pools of standing water that persist through the rainy season at Budalangi (Kenya) and Tororo (Uganda), two high-malaria areas near Lake Victoria, using NISAR L-band radar. The literature reports that malaria risk rises weeks to months after floods, once the shallow pools they leave behind become breeding sites for Anopheles mosquitoes: knowing where water stays, and for how long, helps decide where to look. We detect open water across 17 passes per site, correct a calibration bias between the two orbits, remove permanent water and filter by terrain, giving 205 and 165 candidate pools with their coordinates, water duration and pass-by-pass history. We also tested and discarded our own under-vegetation method, which measured soil moisture. This is NOT a validated malaria risk map: we have no case data at these sites to test the link. The interface presents the results, the evidence and the limits.
details:
What does the project do?

Using NISAR L-band radar, it maps the temporary pools of water that persist after the rains around Lake Victoria, at Budalangi (Kenya) and Tororo (Uganda). Each candidate pool is a precise object: outline, coordinates, area, minimum water duration, elevation, slope, shape and the share of the pool under water at each pass.

Why does it matter?

Anopheles mosquitoes, the vectors of malaria, lay their eggs in stagnant water. The literature reports that malaria risk typically rises weeks after floods, once the shallow, sunlit pools they leave behind have become breeding sites (Gavi VaccinesWork), and a study of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa found that floods increased prevalence two to three months later (Carlson, Carleton et al., Nature 2026, as reported by Carbon Brief). What matters is not the flood itself but the water that stays behind. The rainy season is cloudy: only radar sees through clouds, day and night. These are general findings that we have not tested at our two sites, for lack of case data; this map is meant to tell where to look, and when, so that health data can be used to test the link.

How does it work?

1) 17 NISAR L2 GCOV passes (HH and HV, 10 m) per site, from 25 June to 11 October 2026, on two orbits.

2) We correct a 1.3 dB calibration gap between the two orbits: at Budalangi the descending orbit classified 1.7 times more water than the ascending one; after correction the ratio drops to 1.04.

3) Open water: a dark echo in both HH and HV. Permanent water (the lake) is removed with NISAR_WATERMASK.

4) Duration: the longest run of consecutive passes under water, as a lower bound (one pass every 12 days per orbit).

5) Terrain filter (NISAR_DEM): away from the shoreline, low and flat ground.

Result: 205 pools (144 ha) at Budalangi and 165 pools (87 ha) at Tororo. A shape indicator flags narrow strips, which may be a stream or a ditch.

What we checked, and discarded

We had tested a method to detect water under vegetation. A control test showed that it reacts to rain just as strongly on dry ridges as on the plain: it was measuring soil moisture. We removed it from the result. We also measured that open water outside the lake decreases when it rains, so the correlation with rainfall does not validate the detection, and the interface says so.

Limitations

No health validation: we have no case data at these sites, so the link between persistent water and cases is not tested here. Agreement of only 0.15 to 0.16 with OPERA DSWx outside permanent water (measured at Budalangi). Rice paddies are not separated. Short time series (one semester). Rainfall comes from a Meteomatics trial access, which is not a NASA source. Candidate pools are an indicator of possible exposure, not proof of breeding sites.

Interface

Interactive web application (React, MapLibre): a timeline of passes, a pool-by-pool view with a detailed card and filters, then sections on method, evidence and limitations.

Transparency on AI use

The code, the analysis and the texts of this project were produced with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code. The results were checked against real NISAR files.
